## 1. The numbers
Risk-off. Rate-sensitive tech led the declines while yields and the US dollar rose. Fear gauges also moved higher.

## 2. What moved and why
**Tech leads the slide as AI worries and Nvidia turmoil drag on**
Why it happened: Doubts about AI spending and earnings, plus Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, have kept US stocks turbulent.
Why it matters: Chips and AI names carry much of the market's value, so their weakness drags on the whole index.

**Treasury yields push back above 5% on Fed hike bets**
Why it happened: Hot inflation data and hawkish Fed comments pushed yields up.
Why it matters: The 10-year yield influences borrowing costs across the economy, especially mortgage rates.

**Softer Canadian CPI fails to dent Bank of Canada hike bets**
Why it happened: The Canadian dollar and bond yields fell after a modestly softer-than-expected inflation report, but December hike bets held fairly steady.
Why it matters: The loonie and Canadian bond yields now depend on how sticky inflation proves.

Today's Nasdaq drop is deeper than the S&P's, which fits the same pattern. Higher yields hurt growth companies most. A higher discount rate weighs hardest on long-duration growth stocks. The results will test whether AI demand is holding up. Fed Chair Warsh's noon remarks could move the rate side of the story first.

intern.headline: Stocks slide as bond yields climb on Fed worries
intern.mood: Risk-off. This means investors are scared and are selling riskier assets (like shares) to hold safer ones. Tech stocks, which are sensitive to interest rates, led the drop. Bond yields (the interest rate paid on government loans) and the US dollar both rose. Fear gauges (measures of how nervous investors are) also moved higher.

stories.title: Tech leads the slide as AI worries and Nvidia turmoil drag on
stories.why_happened: Doubts about AI spending and earnings (how much profit companies make), plus Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia (the chipmaker), have kept US stocks shaky.
stories.why_matters: Chips and AI companies make up a big share of the market's total value (the combined price of all its shares), so their weakness drags down the whole index (a basket of stocks used to track the market).
stories.full: Tech has been the weak spot for weeks. Nvidia was down nearly 30% from early October as of last Tuesday. Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer says AI stocks sit more than 30% below their highs. A smaller-than-expected Anthropic valuation (the price investors put on the AI company Anthropic) also weighed on the sector last week. Friday brought more of the same. The S&P 500 (an index of 500 large US companies) fell 0.4% and the Nasdaq (an index heavy in tech companies) fell 0.9%. AMD lost 8.8% and Broadcom 4.8%. Today's Nasdaq drop is deeper than the S&P's, which fits the same pattern. Higher yields hurt growth companies most. A higher discount rate (the rate used to value future profits today) weighs hardest on long-duration growth stocks (companies whose big profits are expected far in the future). Companies with near-term cash flows (money coming in soon) are less exposed. Heavy AI spenders and their suppliers face the most scrutiny. Next up is the earnings calendar (the schedule of company profit reports). Nvidia reports Tuesday evening. The results will test whether AI demand is holding up. Fed Chair Warsh's noon remarks could move the rate side of the story first.

stories.title: Treasury yields push back above 5% on Fed hike bets
stories.why_happened: Hot inflation data (prices rising faster than expected) and hawkish Fed comments (signals that the central bank may raise rates) pushed yields up.
stories.why_matters: The 10-year yield (the interest rate on 10-year US government loans) influences borrowing costs across the economy, especially mortgage rates (the interest rate on home loans).
stories.full: The selloff began with last Tuesday's inflation report. Core inflation (prices excluding food and energy, which can swing a lot) rose 0.3% on the month, against 0.2% expected. Fed Governor Chris Waller said he would consider a 50 bp (half a percentage point) hike in December if core inflation keeps printing 0.3% or higher. The two-year yield jumped as much as 37 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) last week. Markets are now pricing a longer rate-hike cycle (a series of rate increases spread over time). The odds of a December hike were 89% on Nov. 10. Bonds are no longer cushioning equity losses. Yields had fallen from 5.36% to 4.86%, which briefly made bonds a hedge (an investment that helps protect against losses elsewhere) against the AI selloff. They have since rebounded. Borrowers and growth stocks lose when yields rise. Savers and short-term bond buyers gain. Watch Tuesday's US retail sales (how much shoppers spent) and Wednesday's Fed minutes (the written notes from the central bank's last meeting), which IC calls arguably the key event of the week.

stories.title: Softer Canadian CPI fails to dent Bank of Canada hike bets
stories.why_happened: The Canadian dollar (the loonie) and bond yields fell after a modestly softer-than-expected inflation report (CPI, the main measure of consumer prices), but bets on a December rate hike held fairly steady.
stories.why_matters: The loonie and Canadian bond yields now depend on how sticky inflation (prices that stay high and do not easily come down) proves.
stories.full: Canada's October CPI landed this morning. Economists expected a 0.3% monthly rise and 3.2% year over year (compared with the same month last year). The print came in a bit softer. The loonie slipped to 69.89 US cents, and the two-year yield fell about 4 bps (basis points, hundredths of a percentage point) to 3.317%. intern.takeaway: When interest rates and bond yields rise, fast-growing tech stocks often fall, because their future profits are worth less today.
intern.takeaway_accounting: When yields rise, the discount rate used to value future cash flows goes up, which lowers the present value of growth companies' earnings.
intern.takeaway_consulting: Clients with heavy borrowing or long-dated growth assets are most exposed when rates rise, so watch rate moves as a key risk driver.
